transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Ryan Cho (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lydia Chen (Petal Finance - Head of ML), Marcus Riley (Petal - CTO), Priya Nair (Petal - Infra)

Summary: quick discovery focused on unit economics for LLM features (chat + embeddings) and whether Petal should start on Redwood Hosted or go Dedicated / Private later. Key constraints: strict budget for Q4 pilot, latency SLOs for customer-facing chat, and data residency concerns for logs.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching + KV cache levers, quantization/cost tradeoffs, dedicated reserved capacity vs hosted burst, SOC2 + KMS questions, next steps for benchmark run.

Transcript:
[00:00:01] Ryan Cho: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Ryan from Redwood, this is Samir our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:07] Lydia Chen: Good thanks, can hear you. quick heads up we're on a bit of a timebox, 40 minutes.
[00:00:11] Ryan Cho: Totally, we'll keep it tight. Our goal today is to understand your usage, budget, and help figure out hosted vs dedicated.
[00:00:20] Marcus Riley: Great. To start high level -- we run chat for merchant support and some embeddings for search ranking. Pilot target is 2k daily active users, ~100k tokens/day initially, scale to 2M tokens/day in Q1. Budget for pilot is roughly $6k/month.
[00:00:38] Samir Patel: Thanks Marcus, that helps. Quick clarifying question on latency SLOs for chat?
[00:00:45] Lydia Chen: We want p95 under 700ms for short prompts (<=256 tokens). Higher gen tasks can be more lenient. Also need exact-match privacy on logs — certain transcripts cannot leave our VPC.
[00:00:55] Ryan Cho: Good to know. So two surfaces: 1) cost per token for hosted, 2) what Dedicated gets you in terms of predictable unit cost and isolation, and 3) batching/caching levers that can reduce unit cost while preserving latency.
[00:01:08] Samir Patel: I'll give a quick framing — hosted is pay-as-you-go: per-token price plus optional embedding unit rates. Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity with a monthly commit that amortizes into lower per-token cost at scale. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for when you need the control and data residency and includes platform fees.
[00:01:26] Lydia Chen: Do you have example numbers? We tried some runs on OpenAI and it blew our budget.
[00:01:31] Ryan Cho: Sure here's a simple example. For a standard open model on hosted, list price is $0.0006 per token for generation and $0.0001 per token for embeddings — ballpark. At 100k tokens/day that's ~ $60/day or $1.8k/month. But that is raw; we can talk about batching and KV cache
[00:01:49] Marcus Riley: Wait that sounds higher than we expected; our $6k/month target needs to cover infra and Redwood costs.
[00:01:55] Samir Patel: Right — there are levers. First, batching: if you can tolerate a 20-50ms extra queueing delay for concurrent requests, we can batch many requests on the GPU which reduces tokens processed per-second overhead. Second, KV/prefix caching: for chat where users repeat a lot of context, we can cache key/value states so you only generate new tokens. Third, quantized model variants (int8/4-bit) reduce GPU cost per token.
[00:02:14] Lydia Chen: How do we estimate savings? 
[00:02:16] Samir Patel: Typical real-world savings numbers: batching + improved request shaping can reduce per-token cost 20-40% depending on concurrency and seq length. KV caching for chat with repeated prompts can cut the generation tokens by 30-70% for some flows. Quantization can reduce server-side cost and increase throughput 1.5-2x, lowering unit cost further.
[00:02:33] Marcus Riley: So at our 100k tokens/day baseline, 30% reduction gets us to around $1.2k/mo on hosting for generation alone? Is that right?
[00:02:40] Ryan Cho: Roughly. Remember embedding costs and also inference overhead (concurrent context, active sessions). For a pilot we recommend running a short benchmark with your traffic trace so we can simulate batching and cache hit rates. That will produce a per-token effective cost estimate, not just list price.
[00:02:55] Priya Nair: On dedicated — what's the commit size and how quickly can we scale? We don't want to overcommit.
[00:03:02] Samir Patel: Dedicated comes in SKU blocks (e.g., 8-GPU cluster unit) with monthly or annual commitment. For small pilots we also offer smaller reserved pools or burst capacity on top of a smaller commit. The pricing math is essentially monthly fixed cost / expected token throughput => effective per-token cost. At low volumes hosted is often cheaper; Dedicated becomes attractive once you're sustaining several hundred million tokens/month.
[00:03:25] Lydia Chen: Our forecast doesn't hit hundreds of millions till late Q2. So maybe hosted for pilot and Dedicated later. But we need data residency for some transcripts — can hosted keep logs in our region and integrate with our KMS?
[00:03:36] Ryan Cho: Hosted can support region-specific deployments and integrate with customer-managed KMS for encryption of stored artifacts in the Private plan. For hosted we offer regional isolation and strict retention windows, but if transcripts cannot leave your VPC, that's where Private/VPC or on-prem becomes necessary.
[00:03:52] Marcus Riley: So data residency might push us to Private for payment flows; otherwise chat transcripts may be okay on hosted if we set retention to zero and route via our VPC egress?
[00:04:01] Samir Patel: You can also use tokenization and PII redaction pre-ingest to avoid sending sensitive fields. But yes, Private gives the strongest guarantee. There's a tradeoff: Private has higher fixed platform fees and integration overhead.
[00:04:13] Lydia Chen: Back to cost math — can you walk us through an example comparing hosted vs small dedicated commit for our 2M tokens/month near-term target?
[00:04:22] Ryan Cho: Sure. Hosted: assume net effective generation price after caching/batching 0.00045 per token. At 2M tokens that's $900/mo. Embeddings maybe 200k tokens at 0.00009 = $18. Total approx $918/month. Dedicated: an 8-GPU reserved unit might be $X/month (Samir will fill in), amortized across expected tokens. If you only use 2M tokens, the fixed commit likely drives a higher per-token cost. The break-even tends to be above 30-50M tokens/month for full 8-GPU units, depending on model and quantization.
[00:04:50] Samir Patel: To add numbers: a small dedicated pool (scaled to your pilot) could be structured as a smaller reserved + burst. For example, a minimal commit might be $6k/month for a small GPU pool that would give an effective per-token cost of ~$0.00015 if you hit ~40M tokens. But at 2M tokens it would be $3.0/token-equivalent? sorry I mean $3K/month effective for low usage, so hosted is cheaper at this scale. The spreadsheet I'll send shows break-even curves.
[00:05:15] Marcus Riley: That aligns with our intuition. Our concern is spikes: if we have a day with 10x traffic, hosted may spike cost unpredictably. How do you mitigate that?
[00:05:24] Ryan Cho: We provide quota controls, soft/hard limits, and route-based throttling. Also you can set up auto-burst policies that use a combination of dedicated and hosted fallback. For example Dedicate for baseline and hosted for burst or vice versa. Smart routing helps keep cost predictable.
[00:05:38] Priya Nair: On caching — our chat has many repeated system prompts, can we get specifics on how KV cache will be measured?
[00:05:44] Samir Patel: We'll instrument cache hit rates during the benchmark. The KV cache stores past attention key/value states so decoder doesn't recompute prefix tokens. We measure hit rate and effective tokens generated. In practice for support chat, we see 40-60% token reduction if sessions reuse context. You can also precompute embeddings for static content.
[00:06:02] Lydia Chen: Any limits on simultaneous sessions? We expect many short sessions concurrently morning rush.
[00:06:08] Samir Patel: Concurrency is a function of instance count, batching window, and model latency. For short prompts with small seq lengths, batching gives great throughput. We'll run a simulated concurrent trace to estimate p95 latency given desired batching windows.
[00:06:20] Marcus Riley: Security questions — you mentioned KMS integration and SOC2. Do you have SOC2 report and pen-test summaries we can share?
[00:06:27] Ryan Cho: Yes we have SOC2 Type II and pen test summary; I'll attach them. For Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM; hosted supports BYOK for certain artifacts.
[00:06:36] Priya Nair: Network architecture — how would logging and audit trails work? We need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM and long term retention in our bucket.
[00:06:43] Samir Patel: Audit logs can be exported; for Private we forward directly. For hosted we store logs in region with configurable retention and can stream to your S3 or an event bus. We'll share the architecture diagram.
[00:06:54] Lydia Chen: Ok next steps — we'll send a 7-day traffic trace including token lengths and concurrency, you run a benchmark and return an effective per-token price and a recommended config.
[00:07:03] Ryan Cho: Perfect. We'll also include a pricing calc that models batching/cache savings and break-even for Dedicated.
[00:07:07] Marcus Riley: Timeline — can we get the benchmark results by next week? We have an exec review on 2026-09-24.
[00:07:12] Samir Patel: We'll prioritize and aim for 2026-09-22 with the benchmark run and initial slides on 9/23.
[00:07:18] Lydia Chen: Sounds good.
[00:07:20] Ryan Cho: Great, any final questions?
[00:07:23] Priya Nair: One more — does Redwood support per-route model pinning so our fraud flows always use a higher-capacity model?
[00:07:30] Samir Patel: Yes, route-level pinning and canary rollouts. You can pin certain routes to a higher SLA model instance; routing policies control cost.
[00:07:39] Marcus Riley: That's helpful. Thanks everyone.
[00:07:42] Ryan Cho: Thanks — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet, SOC2 docs, and proposed benchmark slot.
[00:07:48] Lydia Chen: Thanks, bye.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription quality: some technical terms transcribed incorrectly (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache", "int8/4-bit quant" sometimes "int8/4 bit quant"), speaker labels approximate.
